ASK:
When talking through your plan for today, what do you think will be the most important?
Give an example where a specific CRM skill would be used today?

NOTE: Review and expand as needed:
Communication
Clear & Concise: Keep messages brief and specific during critical phases.
Closed-Loop: Always confirm receipt and understanding.
Verbal & Non-Verbal: Be mindful of tone and body language, especially under stress.

Problem-Solving & Decision-Making
FOR-DEC Model: Use structured processes for decisions.
Collaborative: Include team input to find solutions.
Time Management: Assess urgency and engage resources as needed.

Workload Management
Prioritize: Focus on critical tasks during high-stress moments.
Delegate: Distribute tasks to manage workload efficiently.
Automation: Use automation wisely but intervene manually when needed.

Situational Awareness
Monitor Flight Path: Stay aware of aircraft’s position and potential threats.
Anticipate: Includes for key changes (e.g., course, altitude).
Focus: Prioritize safety over secondary tasks.

Leadership & Teamwork
Empowerment: Distribute workload and leverage team strengths.
Role Clarity: Ensure PF and PM roles are clear.
Supportive Leadership: Mentor FOs and foster collaboration in decision-making.

ASK:
What RVR value is considered Low Visibility? FOM 10.1, FCTM 2
ANSWER: Below 1200 RVR (350m) 

What is company policy regarding performing procedures, flow patterns and checklists during low visibility taxi Operations? FOM 10.1
ANSWER: Use extra caution when performing procedures, flow patterns, and checklists during low visibility taxi operations. 

When is the ILS critical area in effect? FCTM 5
ANSWER: Ceiling less than 800 or visibility less than 2 miles. Most ILS installations are subject to signal interference by either surface vehicles or aircraft. To prevent this interference, ILS critical areas are established near each localizer and glide slope antenna. In the United States, vehicle and aircraft operations in these critical areas are restricted any time the weather is reported less than 800 foot ceiling and/or visibility is less than 2 statute miles.

If an airport does not have a Surface Movement and Guidance Control System or low visibility taxi charts and the visibility is below 1200 RVR (350m), can we taxi? FOM 10.1
ANSWER: YES. These airports meet the requirements for lighting, markings and vehicular traffic control.
Airports that seek approval for takeoff and landing operations when the visibility is less than 1200 RVR must have a SMGCS or equivalent ICAO plan. This plan will incorporate additional airfield lighting, markings, and procedures, to control vehicular traffic on the airport. 

Can we taxi to the runway with lower visibility than what is required for takeoff? FOM 10.1
ANSWER: YES. While takeoffs are not currently authorized below 500 RVR, taxiing to the departure runway when conditions are improving may be coordinated with ATC using SMGCS procedures. 

What may be considered when crossing a runway and visibility is restricted? FCOM Vol 1 NP
ANSWER: Using a TCAS mode during Taxi TCAS may interfere with ground radar or airborne traffic TCAS processing rate. A TCAS mode may momentarily be selected in order to display any traffic on final to the active runways when visibility is restricted (unable to see aircraft on final), or when the potential for a runway incursion exists.

ASK:
What is the primary lateral reference on a visual approach? QRH MAN
ANSWER: The runway is the primary lateral reference on a visual approach. This means the pilot should be primarily looking outside.

What is the configuration profile for a Two Engines Inoperative approach? QRH 7
ANSWER: 
Use Flaps 25 and VREF 25 for landing.
Select flaps 10 at glideslope alive. 
Extend the landing gear and select flaps 20 at glideslope intercept, or at final descent point. 
Approaching 1,000’ AGL select flaps 25 and center rudder trim. 

What must be completed before 1,000’ AGL? FOM 10.1
ANSWER: Stabilized Approach. All approaches have a stabilized approach gate of 1000 ft AGL.

ASK:
What Non-ILS approaches are authorized? FCOM Vol 1 L, FCOM Vol 1 SP
ANSWER: Its retrievable from the aircraft navigation database. 
Not authorized are RNAV (RNP) and RNP (AR) titled approaches

What are some accepted methods for programing Non ILS approaches in the FMC? FCOM Vol 1 SP
ANSWER: The FMC, Overlay and Manual Waypoint Entry 

What are some considerations when using Integrated Approach Navigation (IAN)? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4, FCOM Vol 1 NP,
ANSWER: 
ILS with G/S out- G/S must be selected off
Use of IAN is not recommended when an approach has a visual maneuver segment that is not in the FMC database. (Example: JFK RNAV 13L)
This procedure is not authorized using QFE.
IAN does not support automatic landings, the pilot flying must disengage the autopilot and complete the landing manually.

When must we add 50’ to the MDA? FCOM Vol 1 SP
ANSWER: Setting PFD - BARO MINS and MCP - ALT window Whenever possible the approach will be flown to a DA(H). This may require the crew to set 50 feet above the published MDA(H) and treat as a DA(H). This is to prevent a descent below the published MDA(H) in case of a missed approach.

ANSWER: 
LVSA
When cleared for the approach the following will be selected or verified: 
Lateral mode- LNAV or LOC
Vertical mode- VNAV 
Speed intervention- Target speed selection with appropriate additive
A­ltitude set DA or MDA on MCP
When the Missed Approach altitude will be set on the MCP

ASK:
When approach clearance has been received and using VNAV, what are appropriate steps that must be accomplished? FCOM Vol 1 NP
ANSWER: LVSA

Your intention is to manually land, on any approach, what are your considerations on disengaging the autopilot? FCOM Vol 1 L; FCTM 6 
ANSWER: The autopilot must be disengaged before the airplane descends more than 50 feet below minimums unless it is coupled to an ILS glideslope and localizer or in the go-around mode.
Note: When a manual landing is planned from an approach with the autopilot engaged, the transition to manual flight should be planned early enough to allow the pilot time to establish airplane control before beginning the flare. The PF should consider disengaging the autopilot and disconnecting the autothrottle 1 to 2 nm before the threshold, or approximately 300 to 600 feet above field elevation.

ASK:
When is TO/GA armed? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4
ANSWER: TO/GA is armed when flaps are out of up or glideslope is captured.

For a Go Around on or near the ground, what briefing item must be included? FCOM Vol 1 NP
ANSWER: Note: Approach briefing must include a reminder that go-arounds on or near the ground require go-around thrust to be set manually and that a flap configuration warning can sound. 

If FLCH is selected during the go around what actions must the PF make?  FCOM Vol 1 NP
ANSWER:  
If FLCH is selected, set speed to the maneuvering speed for the planned flap setting.
After flaps are set to the planned flap setting and at or above the flap maneuvering speed, if FLCH was selected, push the THRUST switch. 

When is a Go Around no longer an option? FCTM 5, FOM 10.1
ANSWER: 
WARNING: Once reverse thrust is initiated following touchdown, a full stop landing must be made. If an engine stays in reverse, safe flight is not possible.
NOTE Once reverse thrust is initiated following touchdown, a full stop landing must be made.

What is your initial target pitch attitude during the Go Around? FCOM Vol 1 NP; FCTM 5
ANSWER: 15 degrees

A roll mode is normally selected at what altitude? QRH MAN
ANSWER: 400 ft AGL

What is the latest point at which a go around can be initiated?  FOM 10.1
ANSWER: Once reverse thrust is initiated, a full stop landing must be made.

ANSWER: Unstabilized approach

ANSWER: The PM must verify that the thrust is sufficient for the go-around or the PF must adjust the thrusts as needed.

ASK:
During a go around near or on the ground what is a precaution the crew must remember? FCOM Vol 1 NP
ANSWER: Warning! TO/GA function is inhibited close to the ground and after touchdown. If the thrust levers do not respond when TO/GA is pushed, or if the go-around is initiated after touchdown, advance the thrust levers manually to go-around thrust.

During an automatic Go Around Procedure what is a consideration the crew should be aware of regarding control inputs? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4, FCOM Vol 1 SP
ANSWER: Thrust and rudder
TO/GA mode termination: above 400 feet radio altitude, select a different roll or pitch mode; all autopilots, except first in CMD, disengage If autopilot systems are compensating for an asymmetric thrust condition when they revert to a single autopilot configuration, the rudder returns to the trimmed position unless the pilot exerts the rudder pedal force required to maintain the rudder position. 
During a multi channel autopilot go-around, the autopilot may disengage unless a new roll or pitch mode is engaged, or a new airspeed is selected prior to approximately 1000 feet above field elevation. If the autopilot disconnects during an engine out go-around, loss of autopilot rudder control can result in large yaw and roll excursions. 

During the go around, what rate of climb does the first press of the TO/GA switches provide? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4
ANSWER: 2000 ft/min

Vertical mode is selected at what altitude? FCOM Vol 1 NP; QRH MAN
ANSWER: 1000 ft AGL (acceleration height). A vertical mode may be selected by the pilot above 400 ft AGL.   

CRM/TEM: 
ASK:
When may go-around thrust have to be set manually? FCOM Vol 1 NP 
ANSWER: On or near the ground. 
Warning! TO/GA function is inhibited close to the ground and after touchdown. If the thrust levers do not respond when TO/GA is pushed, or if the go-around is initiated 	after touchdown, advance the thrust levers manually to go-around thrust.

ASK:
Why do we center the rudder trim on a 50% inoperative approach? QRH 7
ANSWER: Coordinate thrust lever and rudder movement during landing. 

What indications are the flight directors providing when displayed? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 10
ANSWER: ­Control wheel input required by the pilot. Indicates flight director pitch and roll steering commands.

How can the pilot achieve minimum drag condition? FCTM 1
ANSWER: Primary Rudder Trim Technique It is recommended that the autopilot remain engaged while accomplishing the primary rudder trim technique. 
Trim the rudder in the direction corresponding to the down (low) side of the control wheel until the control wheel indicates level. The indices on top of the control wheel should be used to ensure a level wheel condition. The airplane is properly trimmed when the control wheel is level, (zero index).   

What is the proper thrust reverser usage for 50% loss of power? FCTM 6
ANSWER: All to idle reverser and if needed symmetrical full reverse thrust.

ASK:
When will the pilot perform the Windshear Escape Maneuver. QRH MAN
ANSWER: The following are indications the airplane is in windshear: - windshear warning (two-tone siren followed by "WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR, WINDSHEAR”), or unacceptable flight path deviations.

What are the list of unacceptable flight path deviations? QRH MAN
ANSWER: Unacceptable flight path deviations are recognized as uncontrolled changes from normal steady state flight conditions below 1,000 feet AGL, in excess of any of the following: - 15 knots indicated airspeed - 500 FPM vertical speed - 5 degrees pitch attitude - 1 dot displacement from the glideslope - unusual thrust lever position for a significant period of time.

Can the autopilot stay engaged during an automatic windshear maneuver with a stick shaker? Why? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4
ANSWER: 
Automatic Flight Windshear Recovery
With go-around armed, pushing a TO/GA switch commands a pitch-up of 15 degrees or slightly below the pitch limit, whichever is lower. 

With a windshear warning, what happens when the TO/GA switch is pushed? FCOM Vol 2 Ch 4
ANSWER: Windshear pitch mode is activated for vertical guidance. This guidance may pitch up to the Pitch Limit Indicators and result in an intermittent stick shaker.

What are the three areas of action for a crew regarding windshear? FCTM 7
ANSWER: Avoidance, Precautions, and Recovery

slides.t: Approach to Low/High Altitude Stall Prevention and Recovery
slides.n:
ASK:
What are the indications of approach to stall? FCTM 7
ANSWER: The first indication of an approach to stall is the AIRSPEED LOW EICAS message.

When must we recover from a stall warning? FCTM 7 & QRH MAN
ANSWER: 
artificial indication (stick shaker) 
natural indication (initial buffet).

What are the indications of a stall? FCTM 7
ANSWER: An airplane stall is characterized by one or more of the following conditions: 
stall warning 
artificial (stick shaker) 
natural (buffet which could be heavy at times) or
lack of pitch authority
lack of roll control
inability to arrest descent rate.

Is a successful stall recovery dependent on re-engaging the autopilot or autothrottles? QRH MAN
ANSWER: No. The success of this maneuver is not dependent on automation or re-automation in any form. 

Note the following: 
Re-engage the autopilot and activate autothrottle, if desired 
Re-engage automation is if desired. This statement also assumes all the other listed items above this statement has been complied with such as trim, thrust, configuration, appropriate pitch attitude, desired flight path. 
The automation could be one of the driving factors of why the aircraft ended up in the undesired state before the recovery was initiated. 
In every stick shaker event that our operation has seen on the 747 in the past 18 months from (04/14/25) totaling 6. Automation and the desire of the crew to try either remain automated or return to automation has led to additional upsets or stick shakers in the same occurrence. 

CRM/TEM: 
ASK:
Stick shaker and low speed events are occurring more often on the line. What do you think the most significant factor surrounding these events was amongst the crew? Atlas Air 747 stick shaker event reviews - Information obtained from crewmember interviews that experienced approach to stall events in our operation.
ANSWER: First, none of them were expecting a stick shaker, this is understandable for sure. Second and most importantly none of them reacted with the appropriate steps to recover. In some of these events multiple sitckshakers ensued after the first attempt of recovery was made. 

TPO/SPO

ASK:
As a crew, how will you manage a low-speed engine failure while the FO is setting thrust and the Captain’s hand is not yet on the thrust levers? Who calls it out, who decides, and how is control transferred? (QRH: MAN)
Possible Answers:
Brief the RTO in the Takeoff Briefing (FOM 11.1).
Whoever observes the failure calls it out immediately (QRH MAN).
The FO maintains control, reducing thrust as needed, until the Captain makes a positive input to the controls. The Captain announces “REJECT” and assumes control.
The Captain alone decides to reject.

At 20 knots with an outboard engine failed, why is reducing thrust the FO’s primary tool for directional control? (QRH: MAN)
Possible Answers:
The rudder is not yet effective at 20 knots. FCOM Vol 1 NP: “The rudder becomes effective between 40 and 60 knots.”
The other operating outboard engines yaws the airplane. Reducing thrust to all engines removes that asymmetry immediately.
FCTM 3: low-speed directional control after an engine failure “may require all available flight controls until the rudder becomes effective or thrust is reduced on the operating engine.”

Until the Captain makes a positive input, who must maintain control of the airplane, and which callouts belong to the FO after the transfer? (QRH: MAN)
Possible Answers:
The FO maintains control until the Captain makes a positive input (QRH MAN).
After the transfer, per QRH MAN, the FO: 
verifies thrust levers closed, autothrottles disconnected and maximum brakes applied;
calls “Speedbrakes up” or “Speedbrakes not up”;
calls “Reversers normal,” “No reverser engine(s) number ___” or “No reversers”;
calls out any omitted action items;
calls “60 knots”;
communicates the reject decision to the tower and cabin as soon as practical.

CRM/TEM:
